title: Goodwill
hook: the intention of non-ill-will: metta as a steering wheel

segments.voice: Yesterday: nekkhamma, letting go, felt as relief rather than loss. Your line: the relief of less.

In the city of Savatthi, the Buddha says, there lived a lady of the house named Vedehika, and everyone said so: so gentle, so calm, so peaceful. Her maid, Kali, wondered whether that was true, or whether Vedehika had simply never been given a reason to be otherwise. So Kali tested her. One morning she got up late. Vedehika scowled. The next morning, later still: sharp words. The third morning Kali slept in again, and her famously gentle mistress grabbed a rolling pin and hit her on the head. Kali ran out bleeding and told the whole street.
screen: `SO GENTLE, EVERYONE SAID.` → `THE MAID SLEEPS IN.` → `THE THIRD MORNING.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells that story in the sutta of the simile of the saw, and his point is sharp: a person is gentle only until disagreeable words reach them. Being calm when nobody pushes doesn't prove much. That's why the second right intention is goodwill. In Pali it's abyāpāda, literally non-ill-will, and the suttas fill it in with mettā, loving-kindness. Not a warm feeling that washes over you when it likes. An intention: a direction you set. Think of a steering wheel. The road throws things at you: a rude email, a driver who cuts in, a relative who says the thing. You don't control the road. You do have your hands on the wheel, and goodwill is which way you turn it. The same sutta then goes about as far as a teaching can go. Even if bandits were to cut you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, the Buddha says, anyone whose mind filled with hate would not be carrying out his teaching. He tells the monks to train so their minds stay unshaken, they speak no evil words, and they stay with goodwill toward that very person, and from there toward the whole world. Most of us will never meet those bandits. We'll meet the slow line at the pharmacy and the group chat. That may be why the same sutta opens with Vedehika and closes with the saw. The test usually comes in small, ordinary pushes, and each one is a turn of the wheel.
screen: `GENTLE UNTIL SOMEONE PUSHES.` · `ABYĀPĀDA: NON-ILL-WILL.` · `GOODWILL IS A STEERING WHEEL.` · `EVEN UNDER THE SAW.` · then, large: `STEER BY GOODWILL.`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation you'll probably have today with a little friction in it, and picture the moment where it usually goes sideways. Rest your hands lightly, as if on a wheel, and set the direction before it begins: whatever they say, turn toward their good, not agreeing with everything, just the direction. If the old irritation shows up in the picture, notice it, and turn the wheel gently back.
Goodwill. Abyāpāda, non-ill-will, the second kind of right intention: not a mood but a direction you set, close kin to mettā.
Your line: steer by goodwill. You can't control the road, only the wheel. Three hundred sixty-three days, and counting.

howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions practice mettā, often by repeating short phrases of goodwill toward themselves, loved ones, strangers and difficult people; many monastics recite the simile of the saw as a reminder of patience.

fork.setup: you're Vedehika, famous for your calm. your maid has slept in for the third morning running. what does the story say you did?
options: struck her with a rolling pin.
fork.reveal: in MN 21 the famously gentle Vedehika hit Kali on the head; the Buddha's point is that gentleness shows only when someone pushes.

original.note: Pali abyāpāda: non-ill-will, the second of the three right intentions, filled in by the suttas with mettā.

trapdoor: what you thought: goodwill means being nice.
what it means: an intention you set, turning toward the other person's good, tested when they push.

what a scholar hears: the standard definition of right intention (SN 45.8) has three parts, renunciation, non-ill-will and harmlessness; abyāpāda is phrased as an absence, which the suttas fill in with mettā.

chat.says: How can you have goodwill toward someone who's being awful to you?
options: It's a direction you set, not a mood; you can keep steering that way when pushed.
You can't; goodwill is only for people who treat you well in return.
Wait for the warm feeling to arrive; goodwill can't be chosen, it just happens.
chat.meaning: In the simile of the saw, goodwill is an intention you keep, even toward the person pushing you, and from there toward the whole world.

Savatthi.meaning: a great city of the Buddha's time

Vedehika.meaning: a lady known as gentle, until her maid tested her

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21 (Kakacupama Sutta, the simile of the saw)

notes: MN 21 paraphrased: Vedehika and her maid Kali in Savatthi; scowl, angry words, then a blow to the head (rendered 'rolling pin' in common modern translations; confirm the object), Kali goes out bleeding and the neighbors spread the word.

MN 21 saw simile paraphrased: 'even if bandits were to sever you limb by limb with a two-handled saw, one who gave rise to a mind of hate would not be carrying out my teaching', followed by the training to keep the mind unaffected, utter no evil words, and pervade that person and then the world with mettā.
SN 45.8 defines right intention as intention of renunciation, non-ill-will and harmlessness.
howItsDone: the claim that many monastics recite the saw simile is softened; confirm or remove.

Audit (wider sample): the teach said the Vedehika story 'sits next to' the saw simile; in MN 21 the Vedehika story comes early and the saw simile at the end, with other similes between, so the line now says the sutta opens with one and closes with the other. Dropped the stock 'on a Tuesday'.
